title: The Bell at Daybreak
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The water came up through the floor drain before sunrise.

At first I thought somebody had overturned a bucket. The second kitchen was wet around the edges, and a narrow stream of gray water was running toward the back door. The roof repair had held through the rain; the ceiling was dry.

That was worse.

"Iroh," I called.

He came downstairs carrying a lamp.

"Again?"

"Not the roof."

He looked at the drain.

Then he set the lamp on the counter and stopped me from stepping into the water.

"Stay on the dry side," he said. "We do not know what is in it."

I glanced at the shelves. The lowest crate held packaged grain, the next one clean cups. The water hadn't reached the food yet.

We moved everything we could safely reach without stepping into the flood. Iroh closed the kitchen to service and sent a runner to Tamsin. I fetched the emergency sheet we'd prepared after the roof leak, grateful that somebody had insisted on writing it down.

There was a shutoff for the back water line. We turned it.

The water kept rising.

"Then it isn't the supply pipe," I said.

Iroh nodded.

"A drainage problem."

Outside, rain had filled the channels between Jasmine Steps. Water normally flowed away from the terraces toward the old canal. Today it was moving backward, pushing debris through the grates.

Tamsin arrived with Fen and a basket of dry tools.

Fen looked at the tide chart.

"The surge has reached the lower service route. The pressure may be finding the old terrace drains."

I thought of the second bell beneath Tideglass.

"Can we clear it?" I asked.

"Not by climbing into the passage," Fen said. "We need to see where the backflow begins."

Iroh raised the lamp higher.

"The kitchen staff know which drain failed first. We should ask them."

That simple sentence changed the morning.

Mina, who prepared the morning buns, had noticed a gurgling sound near the herb shelf an hour before the water appeared. Bo, who cleaned the pots after closing, remembered the same sound during the last storm, though it hadn't caused a flood then. Neither had mentioned it because they thought the building was old and noisy.

Iroh listened carefully.

"Thank you," he said. "You should have been able to report it without worrying that you'd be blamed."

Mina looked relieved.

We marked the timeline. The sound had started before high tide. It had moved from the rear drain to the small terrace grate, then into the kitchen. Fen compared that with the water levels at the cove. Tamsin checked the accessible inspection covers, refusing to pry open the sealed lower passage until the structural team had a safe plan.

Severus arrived from Moonroot with a copy of the old service drawing.

He put it on the dry table.

"Someone altered the terrace drainage after the Closed Bells," he said. "The original plan shows an overflow branch here."

I looked at the drawing.

A thin line ended beneath the kitchen.

"That's our drain."

"Yes."

"And the branch?"

"Marked as sealed."

Iroh studied the line.

"Then perhaps the water is telling us where the old decision still matters."

Fen nodded.

"We can't reopen the branch today. We can stop the backflow at the accessible upstream junction and use the temporary surface channel."

It was not elegant.

It was safe enough to test.

Danse brought a portable pump. Toph checked the stone support beneath the grate. Edda inspected the alternate route for customers and staff. We set up a temporary service table under the covered terrace so the teahouse could offer simple drinks without asking workers to stand in contaminated water.

Mina made the menu.

Bo posted the closure notice.

Iroh did not insist on serving tea inside the damaged kitchen merely because he was the owner.

By afternoon, the backflow had slowed. The surface channel carried the rainwater away from the building. Tamsin marked the lower drain for repair after the weather cleared.

The kitchen remained closed.

I was exhausted.

Iroh found me sitting beneath the awning with a cup of the ordinary house blend. I had forgotten to drink it until it went cold.

"An excellent temperature for thinking," he said.

I looked at him.

"Do you ever get tired of being wise?"

"Frequently. It is especially tiring when one's feet are wet."

I laughed.

He sat beside me.

"The staff did well," he said.

"They did."

"Mina noticed the first sound. Bo remembered the earlier warning. We would have wasted hours if we'd assumed only the engineers knew what mattered."

I looked at the wet stone terrace.

"That's the thing the vale keeps teaching us, isn't it?"

"Which thing?"

"That every place has people who know something we haven't thought to ask."

He smiled.

"Then perhaps we should make asking a habit."

I leaned against his shoulder.

"Can I ask you something?"

"Of course."

"Are you frightened?"

He considered.

"Yes. This shop is one of the few places I've chosen to build with my own hands after so much loss. I am not ready to lose it to a drain."

I took his hand.

"You don't have to pretend you're calm for me."

"I know."

He kissed my temple.

We sat beneath the awning until the rain became a mist. There were still repairs to arrange, workers to pay, and a kitchen to dry before it could be used. Nothing about the day had been magical.

That evening, Mara sent bread. Greg delivered clean blankets for the staff who had been soaked during the first cleanup. Neri posted a public notice about the drainage inspection, careful not to present a theory as a confirmed cause.

The next morning, the bell sounded once from Lanternwell.

The cove did not answer.

Fen wrote that observation in the log.

The silence was evidence, not a promise.

Iroh made tea on the temporary stove and handed me a warm cup.

"One thing at a time," he said.

For once, I didn't argue.
